name: Ilan Ramon
milestone_by_age_26: Graduated from the Israel Air Force Flight Academy as a fighter pilot at age 20 in 1974, having already served in the Yom Kippur War in 1973.
early_history_summary: Ramon began the IAF fighter pilot course in 1972 at age 18, interrupting it to serve in an electronic warfare unit during the Yom Kippur War. He graduated from the IAF Flight Academy in 1974 at the top of his class and went on to fly A-4 Skyhawks and Mirage III-C jets before becoming part of the first F-16 squadron establishment team by 1980.
family_context_summary: Born to Holocaust survivor parents in Ramat Gan; his mother and grandmother survived Auschwitz, and his father's family fled Nazi Germany in 1935. The family was of modest means and Ramon grew up in Beersheba.
primary_early_advantage_tags: IAF Flight Academy, fighter pilot training, Yom Kippur War, selective military pipeline
evidence_summary: Ramon entered the IAF Flight Academy at 18, served in the Yom Kippur War, and graduated as a fighter pilot at 20 in 1974. The IAF Flight Academy is one of the most selective military training pipelines in the world. His family background as children of Holocaust survivors provided a context of adversity and national duty. By 26 he was part of the first F-16 squadron establishment team in Israel, a materially significant military role.
starting_point: Born in 1954 in Ramat Gan, Israel to Holocaust survivor parents; mother survived Auschwitz, father's family fled Nazi Germany in 1935; grew up in Beersheba in a modest household.
current_position: Died on February 1, 2003 at age 48 when Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry; was Israel's first astronaut and a Colonel in the IAF.

trajectory.event: Graduated from IAF Flight Academy as a fighter pilot, top of his class.
Part of the first F-16 squadron establishment team in Israel, trained at Hill AFB, Utah.
Participated in Operation Opera, the bombing of the Iraqi nuclear reactor at Osirak.
Completed BSc in electronics and computer engineering from Tel Aviv University.
Promoted to Colonel and appointed Head of Department of Operational Requirement for Weapon Development.
Selected by NASA as the first Israeli astronaut, began training at Johnson Space Center.
Died aboard Space Shuttle Columbia (STS-107) when it disintegrated during re-entry on February 1, 2003.

name: Luka Dončić
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2018 EuroLeague championship and EuroLeague MVP at age 19 with Real Madrid, becoming the youngest MVP in EuroLeague history.
early_history_summary: Dončić began playing organized basketball at age 7 in Ljubljana, constantly playing with older children. He joined Real Madrid's youth academy at 13, made his professional debut for Real Madrid's senior team at 16 (youngest in club history), and won the EuroLeague title and MVP at 19 before being drafted 3rd overall in the 2018 NBA Draft.
family_context_summary: Born to Saša Dončić, a Serbian-Slovenian professional basketball player who played for nearly two decades in Slovenia and Europe, and Mirjam Poterbin, a Slovenian model and beauty salon owner. His godfather is former NBA player Rasho Nesterović.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a professional basketball player (18-year career in Slovenia, Serbia, and France) who introduced Luka to the game from infancy. Godfather Rasho Nesterović was a former NBA center. Basketball was a constant in Dončić's early life.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father pro basketball player, Real Madrid academy, early specialization, godfather NBA player, Slovenian basketball culture
evidence_summary: Dončić was immersed in basketball from birth through his father Saša, a professional player for 18 years. He joined Real Madrid's elite youth academy at 13, debuted professionally at 16, and won EuroLeague MVP at 19. His father's career and connections (including godfather Rasho Nesterović) provided direct domain exposure, while Real Madrid's academy offered an elite institutional pipeline. The combination of family-domain apprenticeship and early institutional acceleration produced one of the most precocious basketball careers in history.
starting_point: Born in 1999 in Ljubljana, Slovenia to a professional basketball player father (Saša Dončić) and a model/beauty salon owner mother; grew up immersed in basketball from infancy.
current_position: Plays for the Los Angeles Lakers as of 2025 after a blockbuster February 2025 trade from the Dallas Mavericks; signed a 3-year $165 million contract extension; five-time All-NBA First Team selection and five-time All-Star.

trajectory.event: Made professional debut for Real Madrid in the Liga ACB, youngest player in club history.
Won EuroLeague championship and EuroLeague MVP with Real Madrid; drafted 3rd overall in the NBA Draft by Atlanta (traded to Dallas).
Named NBA Rookie of the Year with the Dallas Mavericks.
Selected to All-NBA First Team for the first time.
Led the Dallas Mavericks to the NBA Finals, averaging near triple-double in the playoffs.
Traded to the Los Angeles Lakers in a blockbuster deal; signed 3-year $165 million extension.

name: Chris Rea
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Rea bought his first guitar at 21, joined a local band in 1973, and won a Melody Maker Best Newcomers Award in 1975 (age 24) but the band failed to secure a record contract. His first solo album was released in 1978 at age 27, and his commercial breakthrough came in the late 1980s.
early_history_summary: Rea grew up working in his family's ice cream business in Middlesbrough and bought his first guitar at 21. He joined the local band Magdalene in 1973, which became the Beautiful Loser and won a national talent contest in 1975, but failed to get a record deal. His first solo album came in 1978 at age 27.
family_context_summary: Born to an Italian immigrant father who ran a well-known local ice cream business (Rea's Creamy Ices) and an Irish mother in Middlesbrough. One of seven children.
evidence_summary: Rea came to guitar late at 21 and spent his early twenties in local Middlesbrough bands. While the Beautiful Loser won a Melody Maker award in 1975, the band could not secure a record contract. His first solo album arrived at 27 and his commercial breakthrough (The Road to Hell, Auberge) came in his late thirties. No material milestone by 26 was found.

name: John Sulston
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Sulston earned his BA from Cambridge in 1963 (age 21) and PhD in 1966 (age 24), then did postdoctoral research at the Salk Institute. His breakthrough work on C. elegans cell lineage began in 1969 at age 27, leading to the Nobel Prize in 2002. No material milestone by 26 was found beyond standard academic credentials.
early_history_summary: Sulston studied natural sciences at Pembroke College, Cambridge on a scholarship, earning his BA in 1963 and PhD in 1966 on the chemical synthesis of DNA. He then pursued postdoctoral research at the Salk Institute before joining Sydney Brenner's group at the MRC LMB in 1969, where his career-defining work began.
family_context_summary: From a modest family; mother from Midlands engineers, father from tenant farmers near Oxford. Received a scholarship to Merchant Taylors school, which was a financial relief for his parents who were not particularly well off.
evidence_summary: Sulston followed a standard academic path through Cambridge (BA 1963, PhD 1966) and a postdoc at the Salk Institute. His Nobel Prize-winning work on C. elegans cell lineage only began in 1969 when he joined Brenner's group at the MRC LMB, at age 27. No independently verifiable material milestone by 26 was identified beyond completing his PhD.

name: Richard Møller Nielsen
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Møller Nielsen played as a defender for Odense BK (1955-1962) and earned two caps for Denmark's amateur national team (1959-1961), but his career-ending knee injury came at 25. His material fame came as a coach, leading Denmark to the 1992 European Championship at age 55. Two caps for an amateur side is not a material milestone.
early_history_summary: Møller Nielsen joined Odense Boldklub at 12 after the 1948 Olympics inspired him. He played for OB's first team from 1955 to 1962, earning two senior caps for Denmark. A severe knee injury in a 1961 international match ended his playing career at 25, after which he transitioned to coaching.
family_context_summary: Born in 1937 in Store Ubberud near Odense, Denmark, the youngest child in a family not interested in sports. His parents were not particularly well off.
evidence_summary: Møller Nielsen was a modest defender for Odense BK who earned only two caps for Denmark's all-amateur national team before a knee injury ended his playing career at 25. His material success came decades later as a coach, winning Euro 1992 at age 55. Two caps for an amateur side does not constitute a material milestone by 26.

name: Adam Małysz
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first Ski Jumping World Cup event in Oslo on March 17, 1996 at age 18, followed by multiple World Cup victories in Sapporo and Hakuba in January 1997 at age 19.
early_history_summary: Małysz took his first ski jump at age 6 in his hometown of Wisła, a town with deep ski jumping traditions. His great-grandfather built a ski jump, his uncle Jan Szturc was a ski jumping coach, and his father was a driver at the local ski club. He debuted in the World Cup at 17 in January 1995 and won his first World Cup event at 18 in March 1996.
family_context_summary: Born in Wisła, Poland to Ewa and Jan Małysz. His family had deep ski jumping traditions: his great-grandfather Andrzej Szturc built a ski jump before WWII, his uncle Jan Szturc was a ski jumping coach, and his father was a driver at the local ski club. The family was working-class; Małysz attended vocational school to learn tinsmith-roofing.
parent_family_domain_summary: Multi-generational ski jumping family: great-grandfather built a ski jump, uncle Jan Szturc was a ski jumper turned coach who was Małysz's first trainer, and his father was a driver at the local ski club. The family lived in Wisła, a town where ski jumping was a way of life.
primary_early_advantage_tags: ski jumping family tradition, Wisła ski jumping culture, uncle as coach, early specialization, working-class background
evidence_summary: Małysz was born into a multi-generational ski jumping family in Wisła, Poland, a town where the sport was a local tradition. His great-grandfather built a ski jump, his uncle was his first coach, and his father worked at the ski club. He started jumping at 6, debuted in the World Cup at 17, and won his first World Cup at 18. The combination of family-domain apprenticeship and frontier geography immersion (Wisła as a ski jumping heartland) produced one of the greatest ski jumpers in history.
starting_point: Born in 1977 in Wisła, Poland to a working-class family with deep ski jumping traditions; father was a driver at the local ski club, mother's family had multi-generational ski jumping heritage.
current_position: Retired from competitive ski jumping in 2011; now a rally driver competing in the Dakar Rally and Cross Country events; widely regarded as the most successful ski jumper in history with four World Cup titles and four Olympic medals.

trajectory.event: Won his first Ski Jumping World Cup event in Oslo on March 17, 1996.
Won World Cup events in Sapporo and Hakuba, establishing himself on the international circuit.
Won the Four Hills Tournament and his first overall World Cup title, beginning a period of dominance.
Won two Olympic silver medals at Salt Lake City and his second consecutive World Cup title.
Won his third consecutive World Cup overall title.
Won his fourth overall World Cup title.
Won Olympic silver and bronze medals at the Vancouver Winter Olympics.
Retired from competitive ski jumping; transitioned to rally driving.

name: Nick Ut
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1973 Pulitzer Prize for Spot News Photography at age 22 for 'The Terror of War' (Napalm Girl), one of the most iconic photographs of the 20th century, taken on June 8, 1972 when he was 21.
early_history_summary: Ut was hired by the Associated Press Saigon bureau in 1966 at age 15, replacing his older brother Huynh Thanh My who was killed covering the Vietnam War. He started in the darkroom and began shooting in the field by 1968 at age 17. On June 8, 1972, at 21, he took the Napalm Girl photograph and won the Pulitzer Prize the following year at 22.
family_context_summary: Born in Long An, Vietnam in French Indochina as the 11th of 12 children. His older brother Huynh Thanh My was an actor-turned-AP photographer who was killed by the Viet Cong in 1965, directly leading to Ut's hiring by AP at 15.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. His brother Huynh Thanh My taught him photography and was an AP photographer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: brother killed in war, AP Saigon bureau, war zone immersion, Pulitzer Prize at 22, Vietnam War
evidence_summary: Ut's entry into photojournalism was catalyzed by his brother's death covering the Vietnam War for AP in 1965. Hired at 15 by AP's Saigon bureau, he grew up in a war zone, developing combat photography skills through direct immersion. The AP Saigon bureau was the world's elite conflict photography pipeline. His Pulitzer Prize at 22 for the Napalm Girl photograph made him the youngest Pulitzer-winning photographer. The adversity of losing his brother and growing up in a war zone was a powerful constraint-driven catalyst.
starting_point: Born in 1951 in Long An, Vietnam (French Indochina) as the 11th of 12 children; his older brother was an AP photographer killed in the Vietnam War in 1965.
current_position: Retired from the Associated Press in 2017 after 51 years; living in Los Angeles. The authorship of his most famous photograph (Napalm Girl) has been disputed since a 2025 documentary, though AP maintains the attribution.

trajectory.event: Hired by the Associated Press Saigon bureau, replacing his killed brother.
Took 'The Terror of War' (Napalm Girl) photograph on June 8, 1972, one of the most iconic images of the Vietnam War.
Won the Pulitzer Prize for Spot News Photography and World Press Photo of the Year.
Relocated to AP's Los Angeles bureau after the fall of Saigon.
Retired from the Associated Press after 51 years of service.

name: Edurne Pasaban
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Pasaban began rock climbing at 15, climbed Mont Blanc at 16, and attempted Dhaulagiri in 1998 at age 25 without reaching the summit. Her first 8,000-meter peak summit (Everest) was on May 23, 2001 at age 28. No material mountaineering milestone by 26 was found.
early_history_summary: Pasaban began rock climbing at 15 with her cousin in the Basque Country, climbed Mont Blanc at 16, and traveled to the Andes at 16-17. Her first Himalayan expedition was in 1998 at age 25, attempting Dhaulagiri without summiting. She summited her first 8,000-meter peak (Everest) in 2001 at 28.
family_context_summary: Born in Tolosa, Gipuzkoa in the Basque Country to a family of businessmen; grew up beside the family's paper-cutting machine manufacturing company (PASABAN S.A.), an international market leader. She worked as an engineer in the family business.
evidence_summary: Pasaban's mountaineering milestones came after age 26: her first 8,000-meter summit (Everest) was in 2001 at age 28, and she became the first woman to climb all 14 eight-thousanders in 2010 at 36. While she had significant mountaineering experience before 26, including a Himalayan attempt on Dhaulagiri in 1998, she did not summit any major peak by that age. Her family's business resources likely supported her expeditions but no material milestone by 26 was identified.

name: Marlene Dumas
milestone_by_age_26: Had her work included in a group show at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam in 1978 at age 25, with her first museum sale ('Don't Talk to Strangers') purchased by the Stedelijk, one of Europe's premier modern art museums.
early_history_summary: Dumas grew up on a wine farm in Kuils River, South Africa, and enrolled at the University of Cape Town's Michaelis School of Fine Art in 1972, earning her BA in 1975. She moved to the Netherlands in 1976 on a scholarship to study at Ateliers '63 in Haarlem, an elite artist-run postgraduate program. In 1978, she appeared in a group show at the Stedelijk Museum and made her first museum sale.
family_context_summary: Born in 1953 in Cape Town, South Africa, and grew up on a family wine farm in Kuils River. Her father ran the family winery and died when she was 12. The family was Afrikaans-speaking. She moved to the Netherlands in 1976, partly due to the Soweto Uprising and the linguistic similarity between Dutch and Afrikaans.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Ateliers '63, Stedelijk Museum, University of Cape Town, Amsterdam art scene, apartheid context
evidence_summary: Dumas leveraged an elite educational pipeline from the University of Cape Town's Michaelis School to Ateliers '63, an exclusive postgraduate studio program in the Netherlands. By 25, she had a group show at the Stedelijk Museum and her first museum purchase. Growing up under Apartheid as an Afrikaans woman and losing her father at 12 shaped her distinctive artistic perspective. Her move to Amsterdam placed her in a frontier art ecosystem, though her early group show was 'barely noticed' by critics.
starting_point: Born in 1953 in Cape Town, South Africa to an Afrikaans family; grew up on a family wine farm in Kuils River; father died when she was 12.
current_position: Lives and works in Amsterdam; widely regarded as one of the most influential painters working today; set the auction record for a living female artist in 2025 with Miss January selling for $13.6 million; represented by David Zwirner gallery.

trajectory.event: Completed BA in Fine Arts from the University of Cape Town's Michaelis School of Fine Art.
Group show at Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam; first museum sale of her work to the Stedelijk.
Participated in Documenta 7 as one of the youngest artists.
First solo museum exhibition at Centraal Museum in Utrecht.
Major retrospective 'Measuring Your Own Grave' at MOCA Los Angeles, traveling to MoMA New York.
Set auction record for a living female artist with Miss January selling for $13.6 million at Christie's.

name: Nils Nilsson
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1957 Ice Hockey World Championship with Sweden at age 21, scoring 10 goals in 7 games. By 26, he had also won a second World Championship gold (1962), been named best forward at the 1960 Olympics, and been selected to the Swedish all-star team multiple times.
early_history_summary: Nilsson grew up in Forshaga, a small industrial town in Värmland, Sweden, where hockey was the dominant local culture. He debuted for Forshaga IF's senior team at 16 in 1952, joined the Swedish national team at 18 in 1954, and was part of the 'Ungdomskedjan' (Youth Line) alongside Ronald Pettersson and Lars-Eric Lundvall. He won his first World Championship at 21 in 1957.
family_context_summary: Born in Forshaga, a small industrial town in Värmland, Sweden. Not documented in reviewed sources as having particular family wealth or domain connections; the town itself was hockey-mad with 4,000-5,000 spectators at home games in a town of 6,000.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Forshaga hockey culture, early senior debut at 16, Ungdomskedjan line, Swedish national team, Värmland
evidence_summary: Nilsson grew up in Forshaga, a small Swedish town where hockey was the dominant social activity, with nearly the entire town attending games. He debuted in the top Swedish league at 16 and was promoted to the national team at 18. His early immersion in a hockey-mad community and rapid promotion through the Swedish hockey system exemplify self-created domain repetition in a frontier geography. By 21, he was a World Champion, and by 26 he had two World Championship golds and an Olympic best-forward award.
starting_point: Born in 1936 in Forshaga, a small industrial town in Värmland, Sweden; grew up in a hockey-mad community where the local team drew nearly the entire town to games.
current_position: Died on June 24, 2017 at age 81 in Karlstad, Sweden. Final role: retired from competitive hockey in 1969 after winning the Swedish championship with Leksands IF; later worked as a product developer at Jofa sporting goods and as a traveling candy salesman.

trajectory.event: Debuted for the Swedish national team, beginning a 205-cap international career.
Won World Championship gold medal with Sweden, scoring 10 goals in 7 games.
Named best forward of the 1960 Olympic hockey tournament in Squaw Valley.
Won second World Championship gold; selected to the World Championship all-star team.
Won Olympic silver medal at the Innsbruck Winter Olympics.
Awarded the Guldpucken as the best Swedish hockey player of the year.
Inducted into the IIHF Hall of Fame.
Died on June 24, 2017 in Karlstad, Sweden.

name: Mikkel Hansen
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Danish handball championship with GOG in 2007 at age 19, made his Danish national team debut the same year, and joined FC Barcelona in 2008 at 20. By 24, he was named IHF World Player of the Year (2011).
early_history_summary: Hansen grew up in Helsingør, Denmark, the son of Flemming Hansen, a Danish international handball player and Olympian (1984). He played youth handball at Helsingør IF and Virum-Sorgenfri HK before joining GOG's senior team in 2005 at 17. He won the Danish championship with GOG in 2007, debuted for Denmark's national team, and moved to FC Barcelona at 20 in 2008.
family_context_summary: Born in Helsingør, Denmark to Flemming Hansen, a Danish international handball player who earned 120 caps, scored 240 goals, and represented Denmark at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. His mother Helle was also supportive of his athletic career. Hansen grew up in the Helsingør arena where his father played.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Flemming Hansen was a Danish international handball player (120 caps, 1984 Olympian) who played the same position (left back) as Mikkel. He served as a guide and mentor rather than a pushy parent, providing advice from his own elite career experience.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father Olympian handball player, GOG talent factory, Danish handball culture, FC Barcelona, early specialization
evidence_summary: Hansen was born into a handball family: his father Flemming was a Danish international with 120 caps and an Olympic appearance. He grew up in the Helsingør arena watching his father play, giving him direct domain exposure from infancy. GOG, Denmark's premier handball talent factory, provided the elite institutional pipeline. By 19, he was a Danish champion and national team player; by 20, he was at FC Barcelona; by 24, he was IHF World Player of the Year. The combination of family-domain apprenticeship and elite institutional acceleration produced one of handball's greatest ever players.
starting_point: Born in 1987 in Helsingør, Denmark to Flemming Hansen, a Danish international handball player (120 caps, 1984 Olympian) who played the same left back position; grew up immersed in the sport from birth.
current_position: Retired from professional handball in 2024 after winning his second Olympic gold medal at the Paris 2024 Olympics with Denmark; widely considered one of the greatest handball players of all time with three IHF World Player of the Year awards.

trajectory.event: Made senior club debut for GOG Håndbold in the Danish Handball League.
Won the Danish championship with GOG; made his debut for the Danish national team.
Joined FC Barcelona Handbol; scored a famous buzzer-beating winner against Russia at the Beijing Olympics.
Named IHF World Player of the Year for the first time.
Won European Championship gold with Denmark.
Won Olympic gold with Denmark at the Rio Olympics, named tournament MVP.
Won World Championship gold with Denmark on home soil.
Won second Olympic gold at Paris 2024 and retired from professional handball.

name: Paolo Conte
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Conte released a jazz EP with the Paolo Conte Quartet in 1962 at age 25, but this was a small-scale release. parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a notary and passionate jazz amateur who encouraged musical education. Conte's brother Giorgio also became a songwriter. Parents were avid jazz fans who defied fascist authorities by playing jazz records during WWII.
evidence_summary: Conte came from a well-to-do family with a jazz-loving father who encouraged musical education, but he practiced law through his twenties and thirties.
